b: What this is # A reference implementation library, not a framework. Each atom is a single Python file you can read in one sitting, next to a Markdown companion that explains the intuition, derives the update rule, names the failure modes and says where the thing is actually the right tool. One file, no framework. and nothing else. No , no pipelines, no hidden preprocessing. Every variant. ships multi-head, MQA, GQA, sliding-window, linear and a tiled flash-style kernel in the same file, behind . The catalog lists 1,300+ named variants across ~250 atoms. Honest documentation. The is not a paper summary. It is what you needed the first time you implemented it, including the part that breaks. The idea: atoms and variants # An atom is an algorithm family: one , one , one mathematical core. A variant is a named specialisation of that core — a different loss, a different regulariser, a different approximation. Variants exist so the repository can be exhaustive without becoming 1,500 micro-files: one place to read the idea, one switch to pick the flavour. b: Losses Intuition # A loss is not a score — it is the estimator . Minimising squared error gives the conditional mean, absolute error gives the median, pinball loss gives any quantile you ask for, cross-entropy gives the conditional distribution. b: Normalisation Intuition # Normalisation removes a degree of freedom you did not want: the scale and offset of each activation. After it, every layer sees inputs with a known mean and variance, so one learning rate works across layers and depth stops multiplying scale error. The textbook reason ("internal covariate shift") is largely wrong — Santurkar et al. showed that BN helps even when the input distribution is held fixed. The mechanism that survives scrutiny is conditioning : normalisation makes the loss landscape smoother (smaller Lipschitz constant of the gradients), which permits larger steps. That is why the layer still helps when the statistics are already stable, and why the placement (before or after the residual add) matters more than the variant. d: Reservoir, alias, stratified, weighted and Gumbel-top-k sampling. Sampling is how a distribution becomes data. Four different jobs get called "sampling", and…
b: Sampling Intuition # Sampling is how a distribution becomes data. Four different jobs get called "sampling", and mixing them up is the usual source of subtle bugs: Draw from a known distribution — inverse CDF, alias, rejection. Draw from a stream you cannot store — reservoir. Draw without replacement or from a truncated distribution — Gumbel top-k, nucleus, negative sampling. Estimate an expectation with fewer draws — stratified, systematic, importance sampling. The first three must be exact; the fourth is allowed to be biased or higher-variance as long as the estimator is right. Keeping that distinction explicit is what separates a sampler from a heuristic. b: Schedules Intuition # A schedule is a statement about how much you trust the current gradient. Early in training the gradient is informative but the model is far from anything good, so you take large steps (after a brief warmup). Late in training the gradient is dominated by noise, and a large step means you never settle. So a schedule has two jobs: get through the transient safely (warmup) and shrink the noise floor (decay). Everything else — restarts, cycles, plateau — is a bet about where the transient ends. A direction supported by a large singular value barely moves; a direction that is almost in the null space (collinear columns, ) gets crushed. That is why ridge is the fix for collinearity and lasso is the fix for "too many features." b: Elastic net Intuition # Lasso has two well-known failures. With it can select at most variables — the support has to be linearly independent. And with a group of highly correlated columns it picks one essentially at random and zeroes the rest, so the selection is unstable under resampling. Ridge has the opposite problem: it never zeroes anything, so it cannot select. The elastic net is the interpolation. Add an term to the lasso objective and the problem becomes strictly convex : the solution is unique, the correlated columns share the weight instead of competing, and the term still produces exact zeros. The term is doing exactly what fails to do when columns are collinear — making all directions equally well-conditioned. b: Nyström approximation — read a kernel from a handful of its rows Intuition # A kernel method never needs the points, only their inner products, and that is usually a gift. Here it is the bill: the inner products are an \(n\times n\) matrix that has to be built, stored and often inverted, so a hundred thousand points is ten billion entries and a kernel ridge fit is a cubic solve. The Nyström method answers the obvious question — do we really need every entry? — by keeping \(m\) rows and reconstructing the rest: The landmarks are rows of the data, so \(K_{nm}\) is one kernel evaluation per pair of a point and a landmark, and \(K_{mm}^{-1}\) is the only inverse — of an \(m\times m\) matrix. Let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto the span of the landmark features. b: CART Intuition # A decision tree asks one question at a time: is feature above or below ? Each answer sends the sample left or right, and the process repeats until a leaf. At each node, every feature is scanned for the threshold whose split most reduces impurity, the best split is taken, and the two children recurse. There is no global optimisation and no backtracking, yet the result is a piecewise-constant function that can approximate any smooth surface to arbitrary accuracy given enough depth. The seven variants are not seven models. The trees are more biased individually but even less correlated, and the ensemble is faster because there is no sort. XGBoost adds the second derivative: every split is scored by how much it reduces a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, and every leaf is set to the Newton step rather than the mean residual. b: Naive Bayes Intuition # Assume the features are independent once you know the class. Then Bayes' theorem collapses from an integral over the joint density into a sum over one-dimensional pieces, and a classifier becomes a table of counts. \[p(c \mid x) \;\propto\; p(c)\,\prod_{j=1}^{d} p(x_j \mid c) \qquad (1)\] The assumption is false for almost every dataset — words in a document are correlated, pixels in an image are correlated, symptoms in a diagnosis are correlated.
